tagline: Quaker houses, divided meeting rooms and a lake that displaced communities.
intro: The Quaker Heritage Scenic Byway makes a 54-mile loop through southwest Ohio. Houses rise above Todd’s Fork, and Caesar Creek State Park adds a lake, beaches and boat docks to the journey. Ohio’s byways program presents the route as a journey into Quaker history and culture, with a pastoral landscape as part of its appeal. The lake also has trails and picnic grounds, while Waynesville brings the route into a town with meetinghouses, a burial ground and a former Friends school.

The Wilmington Lebanon Pike was laid out in 1810 to connect the new Clinton County seat with Lebanon, the older Warren County seat. Early settlers built above the creek; the next generation built beside the new road. Later, construction of Caesar Creek Lake disrupted Quaker communities, closing Caesar’s Creek Meeting and relocating New Burlington Meeting. In 1975, the 1849 Caesar Creek meetinghouse traveled 15 miles to Pioneer Village, where it was set on a new foundation.

Start at the Caesar Creek spillway’s fossil beds, then follow the loop toward the Harvey family house above Todd’s Fork and on to Wilmington. Wilmington College was founded by the Society of Friends in 1870. The return side reaches Waynesville, where the white brick meetinghouse retains two doors and two equal sides.

moments.title: Caesar Creek Spillway and Fossil Bed
moments.text: The Caesar Creek spillway has fossil beds where visitors can examine the region’s geology. Caesar Creek Lake is a twentieth-century addition to this landscape: the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers built the dam in the 1970s. The lake’s construction displaced New Burlington Meeting and brought Caesar’s Creek Meeting to a close. Its 1849 meetinghouse was moved to Pioneer Village in 1975 and placed on a new foundation. The earth-and-rock-fill dam stands 165 feet high and stretches 2,750 feet; construction began in 1971 and finished in 1978.

moments.title: Isaac and Sarah Harvey House
moments.text: The Harvey house is barely visible on the second hill, facing Springfield Friends Meetinghouse across the Todd’s Fork Valley. Caleb Harvey built it in 1848; his son Isaac and daughter-in-law Sarah lived here in the next generation. In the fall of 1862, Isaac and Sarah traveled to Washington to speak with President Lincoln on emancipation. Their son Jesse’s family and then their granddaughter Myra’s family also lived in the house, which was sold out of the family in the late 1980s. Their Washington journey later inspired a statue on the Wilmington College campus.
moments.notice: The house faces Springfield Friends Meetinghouse across the Todd’s Fork Valley.

moments.title: Miami White Brick Meetinghouse
moments.text: Two doors and two equal sides give the 1811 meetinghouse its shape. A partition lowered on rope pulleys divided the interior for separate men’s and women’s business meetings. Quakers began arriving in Ohio by the thousands in 1799, including migrants from North and South Carolina, Pennsylvania and Virginia. Miami Meeting began in 1803 with a log meetinghouse; the larger brick building accommodated the growing Meeting and a Quarterly Meeting drawing several local Meetings together. An 1870 remodeling reduced the building’s height and enlarged its windows. One side now serves worship, the other First Day School and other activities.
moments.notice: The meetinghouse has two doors and two equal sides.
